en: The Sūtra on the Ritual Procedures for the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera, consisting of seventy-two verses,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Dispersing Grandee, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
I pay homage to the Omniscient One, To the sublime Dharma and the Noble Saṅgha.
I shall briefly explain the conduct of a śrāmaṇera To inspire the mind toward renunciation.
Within the teaching of Śākyamuni, One must firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts.
Maintain the precepts as you would protect your own body, guarding them so they are not transgressed.
From rising at dawn until lying down to sleep at night, cleanse your mouth and teeth;
recite mantras until daybreak, and pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Approaching the teacher’s chamber, he lightly knocks on the door with his hand;
having entered, he inquires after the teacher: "Is your body at ease?
Having performed these actions, he then constructs a maṇḍala.
Making offerings with reverence, one should observe the water within jars,
basins, bowls, and other vessels both at dawn and likewise in the afternoon.
Whether the insects in the water are large or small, one should constantly observe them with a sincere mind.
Filter the water through a strainer and examine it closely before using it.
When eating or drinking, maintain a mind of compassion and do not cause harm to insects;
this applies even to those upon plants and trees, or within the cow dung used for smearing the altar.
When using [these things] in this manner, one protects all sentient beings.
Whether within a bed or a seat, or amidst the soil and manure of a field, one observes each and every detail; this is called the practice of renunciation.
Serve the teacher in every way; wash the bowl until it is clean;
perform three prostrations at the proper time; join your palms before the teacher and ask what he shall eat.
Thus, when eating, one should use the previously prepared pure water to rinse the hands for purification; then, in accordance with the Dharma, eat in silence.
Having finished the meal, recite two verses to dedicate the merit to the faithful donor.
Acting in accordance with what has been taught, one increases the practice of right mindfulness.
Believing in and understanding the Dharma of pure precepts, one practices in accordance with the Dharma;
through correct contemplation, one attains personal realization, and the mind of the renunciant finds peace and joy.
If a person violates the precepts themselves, others will see it and treat them with contempt;
both parties incur fault. Therefore, one who maintains the precepts must do so with a single-minded heart.
Whether maintaining the precepts or breaking them—even in the case of those afflicted by illness—[the consequences remain].
If one preaches the Dharma inappropriately to the occasion, others will not value it in their hearts;
at the end of life, they will undergo great suffering.
Furthermore, by performing incantations and the like, one causes others to meet their death.
Furthermore, by employing various skillful means to commit killing,
one creates such causes for breaking the precepts that one will sink forever into the three evil realms;
in hell, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal, one shall receive the retribution of their sins in succession.
Even those among the various classes of devas, if they should likewise kill living beings,
will fall back into the evil destinies and undergo those various evil retributions.
If there are those who have left the household life, yet they indulge their bodies, speech, and minds at will—
If one mistakenly kills ants and the like, one incurs three types of offenses within the three karmas.
If one strikes or hurls earth,
stones, bricks, or tiles at sentient beings, [one likewise incurs such offenses].
Camels, mules, birds, and other such animals— by harming them, one incurs the offense of breaking the precepts.
Likewise, if one arbitrarily mounts and rides camels, mules, elephants, or horses,
or oppresses others by making them carry one back and forth, one also incurs the offense of breaking the precepts.
If there is one who has gone forth, they must not commit theft,
whether by doing it themselves or by instructing another; if they steal property,
even as little as a quarter of a kārṣāpaṇa.
Through such causes of breaking the precepts, one incurs the most grievous offenses.
Whether it be food, drink, grain, and rice, or flowers, fruits, grasses, and trees—
whether growing from the earth or born in water— to steal these things, [is a grave transgression].
Or they may steal official taxes and profits, passing goods privately through customs and ferries;
or they may steal from sentient beings, whether two-footed or many-footed.
Or those who have gone forth as monastics, though their provisions are fully supplied, [may still commit such acts].
If one with a greedy mind further steals wealth, both will incur grave offenses.
If one's own robes, bowl, or other belongings are plundered by thieves, one must not forcibly take them back;
rather, one should transform them through the skillful means of preaching the Dharma.
Or perhaps one turns back from buying; not complying with the whims of others is called the mind of renunciation.
It does not disturb the sores of the three karmas, and the nature of precepts is spontaneously accomplished.
If there are those who have left the household life, they must not engage in sexual desire.
To come of one's own accord out of mutual longing and desire, being deluded and attached,
constitutes the root offense.
Like a snake or like a poisonous drug, it destroys one's own person;
one incurs the suffering of the great hells, is obstructed from nirvāṇa,
and does not emerge from birth and death.
The Perfectly Awakened One is not like this; he has never transgressed the precepts in person. By upholding the precepts, one attains great benefit.
If there is one who has gone forth, they must not utter false speech.
If one says they have seen devas and humans, Speaking with me in conversation,
And that they themselves have also been to the abodes of great beings,
Even to the gandharvas, Respectfully accompanied by nāgas and yakṣas—
The hosts of mahoragas, piśācas, kiṃnaras, and bhūta spirits— those who constantly converse with me—
all speak these words in vain.
Regarding the True Path and the four fruits, one who understands the profound Dharma yet claims to have attained what they have not—
such false speech leads to eternal sinking in the evil realms.
Avoid associating with unwholesome friends, as well as harsh and abusive speech;
do not respond to frivolous talk that confuses right and wrong, nor to various words of contention and strife.
One must endure each and every [difficulty].
If one does not act accordingly, one incurs the offense of violating the precepts;
the wise person maintains them with a single mind, thereby attaining freedom from the faults of verbal karma.
If one uses grains such as rice and the like to brew wine that intoxicates people, one must not drink it intentionally.
Or if one uses sugarcane flowers, grapes, fruits,
and so forth to ferment a beverage capable of intoxicating people, one must not drink it intentionally.
Drinking it oneself or teaching others to drink, one becomes deluded and loses mindfulness;
as the mind of heedlessness increases, the drinker incurs a grave offense.
Therefore the World-Honored One said: "If a person, with a blade of grass or a leaf..."
Dropping wine into one’s mouth increases transgressions; likewise,
going to watch singing, dancing, and prostitutes leads to the commission of offenses against the precepts.
With sandalwood, saffron, and the like, as well as beautiful flower garlands,
gold, silver, and various kinds of jewels, one adorns the body in manifold ways and thereby incurs the offense of violating the precepts.
If one applies decorative marks upon the eyes to make them appear more handsome, one incurs the offense of violating the precepts.
As for seats, couches, beds, and the like, their height should be no more than one cubit;
they must not be made ornate, nor should they be made overly large.
Through heedlessness and failing to act accordingly, one incurs the offense of violating the precepts.
The Buddha taught that those who have gone forth from the household life should distance themselves from such faults.
When receiving food for the fast, it must not be taken after midday.
From sunrise until midday, one may be permitted to receive and eat the meal;
to eat at an improper time, the Buddha said, incurs a grave offense.
If there is a bhikṣu who is ill, he may treat his illness to save his body.
It is permissible to eat after midday;
yet if one is not ill and does not follow the proper time, one incurs the offense of violating the precepts.
One who has left the household life must not touch [food]; for the receiver, it gives rise to craving.
Yet one incurs the offense of violating the precepts.
When making offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha for the sake of generating merit and benefit for others,
it is permissible to accept and enjoy them.
Do not give rise to attachment; if there is anyone who is greedily attached, that person must be expelled.
All forms of frivolous play and laughter, a śrāmaṇera must not engage in; whoever does so incurs an offense.
If one yawns, one should cover the mouth with the hand;
failing to do so incurs an offense.
One should not prostrate without careful consideration; likewise, when novices or others sneeze or spit...
The Elder should offer a blessing: "May you have long life and be free from illness.
When a śrāmaṇera is before his teacher, he must not spit or blow his nose, nor should he brush his teeth.
One must not walk back and forth or sit facing the teacher.
One should honor those of seniority and long-standing virtue in accordance with the Dharma.
When entering the latrine, if someone else is coming from behind, one should alert them with a low voice.
Water filtered to ensure it is free of insects should be used to fill the pure flask;
with hands washed and moving with composure, one does not lose the conduct of a renunciant.
Regarding the teacher’s own seat and bed, one should always use a clean underpad.
Regarding all beds, chairs, and the like, one must not sit upon them as a śrāmaṇera.
If the teacher is absent, one should rely upon pure monks who clearly understand the Vinaya, serving and attending to them.
Do not rely on another community of monks; those who violate this incur an offense.
If a bhikṣu goes abroad for the sake of some business, he shall return within five days;
if he gains a profit, it belongs to the assembly traveling with him.
The same applies to the gains of the assembly; furthermore, if they are given to outsiders after five days have passed, neither party has a share.
When a novice (śrāmaṇera) voids excrement or urine, he must ask whether it is ground belonging to the Buddha or the Sangha.
One must not wander about restlessly; one's conduct should follow the boundaries of one's own domain.
Whatever ordinary tasks one undertakes, one should join the palms and first inquire of the teacher.
By acting in this manner, one does not lose the correct practice.
At sunset, he paid homage to the Buddha’s stūpa; having finished his prostrations, he again questioned his teacher.
He washed his teacher’s two feet, and when these duties were completed, he listened with single-minded attention, gazing expectantly for what was required.
During the first watch and the last watch of the night, do not cease your recitation.
During the middle watch, when you sleep, lie down like a lion.
Practice with a sincere mind; thus you perfume the seeds of the noble ones within your consciousness.
Afflictions will be severed of their own accord, And one will swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
The Sūtra on the Ritual Procedures for the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera, Spoken by the Buddha.
